problem: Classic Embodied Question Answering benchmarks such as EQA-MP3D use templated questions with closed answer vocabularies, which fit poorly with modern open-vocabulary foundation models. No benchmark covered both the episodic-memory setting (e.g., smart glasses recalling past observations) and the active-exploration setting (mobile robots) with free-form natural-language answers.
motivation: An agent that understands its environment should be able to answer arbitrary natural-language questions about it. That ability matters for assistants on smart glasses and for home robots. Foundation models such as GPT-4V now claim strong visual understanding, so a realistic, measurable test of whether they understand 3D environments well enough to answer human questions is needed. Free-form answers also need an automatic evaluation protocol that agrees with human judgement.
key_idea: The paper recasts EQA as open-vocabulary question answering about a real 3D environment, reached either through a recorded episode history (episodic memory) or through active exploration. It releases OpenEQA, a benchmark of 1600+ human-written questions over 180+ real-world scenes, scored by an LLM-based evaluator that correlates well with human judgement.
insight: Current state-of-the-art foundation models, including GPT-4V, fall significantly short of human-level performance. Embodied scene understanding for question answering therefore remains far from solved, and scaling general-purpose VLMs has not closed the gap. An LLM-as-judge protocol can reliably score free-form answers, making open-vocabulary EQA measurable. The abstract alone does not show which question categories or which memory representations are most responsible for the gap.
method: Task formulation: EQA is defined as understanding an environment well enough to answer natural-language questions about it, split into an episodic-memory variant (answer from an agent's past observation history) and an active-exploration variant (the agent must explore to gather information).
OpenEQA dataset: over 1600 human-generated, open-vocabulary question-answer pairs drawn from over 180 real-world environments, supporting both use cases.
LLM-powered evaluation protocol: an automatic LLM-based scorer rates free-form answers against human references and shows excellent correlation with human judgement.
Baseline evaluation: several state-of-the-art foundation models, including GPT-4V, are evaluated on the benchmark and compared with human performance.

setting.backbone: Various frozen foundation models evaluated as baselines, including GPT-4V (benchmark paper; no new trained agent)
setting.training_data: none (benchmark / zero-shot evaluation of foundation models)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB(-D) episode history / video of real-world scenes (episodic memory), or egocentric observations gathered during exploration (active setting); exact details not in abstract
setting.action_space: free-form natural-language answer; the active-exploration variant additionally requires navigation actions (details not in abstract)
setting.simulator: real-world scanned environments; simulator for active exploration not stated in abstract
setting.privileged: episodic-memory setting provides a pre-recorded observation history of the environment; otherwise not stated in abstract

results: State-of-the-art foundation models, including GPT-4V, lag significantly behind human-level performance on OpenEQA. The LLM-based evaluation protocol shows excellent correlation with human judgement. The abstract gives no specific scores.
limitations: The benchmark is relatively small (about 1600 questions over about 180 environments).
Evaluation relies on an LLM judge, which may carry evaluator bias despite its reported correlation with humans.
The paper proposes no new method to close the gap to human performance; it mainly provides a benchmark and baseline evaluations.
